title: Chip X-ray
summary: Read a die like an engineer: name the blocks by their texture, then tell what a chip is for from where its area goes.

links.why: a floorplan is the layout seen from far away
cores, caches and buses become blocks you can see

ideas.how: a large share of many dies is memory placed right beside the cores
a GPU is one small core copied dozens of times
a phone chip has a separate block for each job: camera, video, AI, graphics

tradeoffs.how: cache next to a core is fast but takes area; the floorplan shows how much each chip spent

measures.how: the blocks you see each hold millions to billions of them

then: A die photo shows every transistor and wire by eye: the biggest chip so far, {biggest}, has {biggestTr} transistors.
Single transistors become too small to see; dies are read as blocks of memory, logic and pads.
Phone chips put CPU, GPU, image and video engines side by side, each a block on the floorplan.
AI chips are mostly copies of one core plus memory interfaces; die photos are shared at launch as marketing.
Projection: more chips are split into chiplets, so one package holds several dies, each one block type.

learn.plain: Under a microscope a chip looks like a city seen from a plane. You cannot see the people (transistors), but you can tell the districts apart: memory is neat rows like a housing estate, logic is a jumble like an old town, and repeated cores are identical blocks of flats. How much of the city each district takes tells you what the city is for.
learn.engineer: Die shots resolve blocks, not devices. SRAM and DRAM arrays are bit-cell arrays with regular decoders and sense amplifiers; standard-cell logic is placed and routed by tools and looks random; analog and RF blocks are hand-drawn, with inductors and large matched devices; I/O pads and PHYs sit at the edge where bumps or bond wires land. Area shares track priorities: microcontrollers are dominated by flash, SRAM and analog; data center GPUs by replicated SMs, L2 and HBM PHYs; DRAM dies by arrays (array efficiency is typically above half). The floorplans here are typical arrangements, not any product, and kinds are not drawn to the same scale.

quiz.q: On a die photo, what does a large, perfectly regular grid most likely show?
options: Memory: one cell copied millions of times
quiz.why: Memory repeats one tiny cell, so it looks like a regular grid. Logic placed by tools looks like noise.

quiz.q: A die is mostly flash memory, SRAM and analog circuits, with a tiny CPU. What is it?
quiz.why: A microcontroller keeps its program in flash, works in SRAM and talks to sensors and power through analog circuits; the CPU is small.

quiz.q: Why does an AI GPU look like one tile copied many times?
options: Designers build one core well and repeat it, because the work splits into many identical parts
Every core runs a different program type
quiz.why: AI work is many small, identical multiply-adds, so one well-designed core is copied dozens of times.
